bilingual.notes: HTSB issues standalone 'Kaiapuni Hawaiʻi / Hawaiian Language Immersion' and 'ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi / Hawaiian Language' license fields, which roll up under the canonical 'bilingual' umbrella as heritage/medium-of-instruction credentials. These primarily serve Native Hawaiian / Hawaiian-medium students rather than classified ELs in the Spanish/Asian-language sense; requirements are null pending direct citation of HTSB rules (HAR 8-54 series), which were not reachable from this verification session.

eld.notes: HTSB issues a standalone 'Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages' (TESOL) license field at P-3, K-6, 6-8, 6-12, P-12, and K-12 grade bands. Coursework and a content test are required (Praxis ESOL); program and practicum requirements are null because HTSB's content-area-specific rules pages were not reachable from this 2026 refresh session.

history.title: Hawaii Constitution amended — Hawaiian becomes co-official language with English
history.description: At the 1978 Constitutional Convention voters ratified Article XV § 4 of the Hawaii State Constitution, making Hawaiian (ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi) an official language of the State alongside English — the only U.S. state to officially recognize a Native language at constitutional level. Article X § 4 simultaneously requires the State to promote "the study of Hawaiian culture, history, and language." The 1978 amendments are the constitutional predicate for the Hawaiian-medium (Kaiapuni) public-school program, the HTSB Hawaiian Language Immersion teacher fields that this record codes under bilingual, and the State's bilingual approach to EL students whose home language is Hawaiian or a Pacific-Island language.

history.title: Act 89 lifts the ban on Hawaiian-medium public instruction
history.description: The Hawaii Legislature passed Act 89 (1986) repealing the lingering 1896 prohibition on teaching public school subjects in Hawaiian. Coupled with the 1978 constitutional amendment, Act 89 enabled the Department of Education to establish Ka Papahana Kaiapuni — the Hawaiian-medium public-school program — initially at two pilot sites in 1987 and now at over 20 schools statewide. Act 89 is the operational basis for the Hawaiian Language Immersion teacher fields HTSB issues today and is functionally why Hawaii is coded as a bilingual-program-offering state.

history.title: Hawaii adopts the State Seal of Biliteracy
history.description: Act 224 (SLH 2015 / SB 1394) authorizes a State Seal of Biliteracy for graduating high-school students who demonstrate proficiency in English plus one or more additional languages, including ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi. Hawaii is among the early-adopter states.

history.title: EPAA 29(100) document analysis (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021)
history.description: Leider, Colombo & Nerlino published in Education Policy Analysis Archives 29(100) a comprehensive document analysis of every state and DC's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI teacher-credentialing requirements, professional teaching standards mentions, and EL-percentage figures, based on primary SEA sources collected October–December 2019. The 2019 coding of Hawaii's EL-credentialing landscape is preserved as a temporally-anchored research baseline against which the catalog's later verifications are framed.

history.title: NCES Fall 2021 EL count: 17,353 students (10.0%)
history.description: Per NCES Digest Table 204.20, Hawaii's classified-EL share of public-school enrollment rose to 10.0% in Fall 2021, up from 9.5% in Fall 2020 and 7.0% at its 2016 trough. The state remains a WIDA Consortium member and administers ACCESS for ELLs annually.
